lines.trans: I repeat for everyone, the order is already waiting!
Elena, they heard you perfectly well.
Why then is nobody working?
In my kitchen there is always strict order.
You work too slowly for a restaurant.
Every good dish needs its own time.
Guests do not like to wait long for food.
Our guests appreciate high taste.
I will show myself how one must work!
Great, I will go calmly rest.
Are you abandoning your kitchen to me?
I am sure that you will manage excellently.
Return soon, otherwise I will take the restaurant!
We'll see who stays the winner here!

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'dish', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: This is the restaurant's signature dish.

examples.text: Настоящий повар чувствует каждый вкус блюда.
examples.trans: A real chef feels every taste of the dish.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to throw', forming an aspectual pair with 'бросить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to leave, to abandon') (бросать трубку = to hang up) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Он всегда бросает вещи на пол.
examples.trans: He always throws things on the floor.

examples.text: Не бросайте трубку, умоляю вас! Я перед вами стою на коленях.
examples.trans: Don't hang up, I'm begging you! I'm on my knees in front of you.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable masculine noun meaning 'taste', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('taste, preference') (не в моём вкусе = not my type) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы рад вам помочь. Но вы, к сожалению, не в моём вкусе.
examples.trans: I would be glad to help you. But unfortunately you are not my type.

meanings.note: возвращаться домой = to come back home; к + dative = to someone

examples.text: Запомните: зло всегда возвращается к правителю.
examples.trans: Remember: evil always comes back to the ruler.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'time', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'meeting', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('see you') (in 'до встречи' = until we meet) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Решается ваш вопрос, Клавдия Викторовна! Вы не видите, у меня встреча?
examples.trans: Your question is being sorted out, Klavdia Viktorovna! Can't you see I have a meeting?

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'high', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'until' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('goodbye') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: He talks for a long time.
We'll make it! The president always talks for a long time.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'food', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: В этом ресторане всегда свежая еда.
examples.trans: There is always fresh food in this restaurant.
Oh no, bad food? Does your stomach hurt?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wait', forming an aspectual pair with 'подождать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to expect') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

забрать.gloss: to take back, to take away

meanings.en: to take away, to pick up
meanings.note: забрать заявление = to withdraw a statement
забрать заявление = to withdraw a statement

examples.text: Поговори с Аракеляном. Пусть он заберёт заявление.
examples.trans: Talk to Arakelyan. Get him to withdraw his statement.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'order', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: In the kitchen they are preparing this order.

examples.text: Я делаю всё точно по вашему заказу.
examples.trans: I do everything exactly according to your order.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'otherwise'.
Secondary conversational sense ('differently') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Go, or else you'll be late.

examples.text: Пятьдесят метров, не больше. Иначе будет сигнал.
examples.trans: Fifty metres, no more. Otherwise there'll be a signal.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'every', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: in the instrumental: 'кем ты работаешь?'

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to love, to like', paired with 'полюбить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to like') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('my') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary
meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'it is necessary'.

examples.trans: We need to do even more.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
needs 'не' with the verb: никто не войдёт

examples.trans: I know the town like nobody else.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: short form 'нужен / нужна / нужно / нужны' + dative: 'мне нужна работа' = I need a job
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: ничего не осталось = there's nothing left
Secondary conversational sense ('to stay') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

отдохнуть.gloss: to have a rest; to relax

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'дохнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a rest', forming an aspectual pair with 'отдыхать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to vacation') (to take time off) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You need to have a proper rest at home.

examples.text: Иди уже скорее домой, пора хорошенько отдохнуть.
examples.trans: Go home already quickly, it is time to have a good rest.

examples.text: Ложись спать, тебе надо хорошо отдохнуть.
examples.trans: Go to sleep, you need to rest well.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.
Secondary conversational sense ('great!, excellent!') (as a one-word reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I know this town really well!

meanings.note: Agentive or instrument masculine noun meaning 'winner', declining across all six Russian grammatical cases.

examples.trans: The winner received a gold medal.
The name of the grand winner.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'вторять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to repeat, to review', paired with 'повторить'.

examples.text: Ещё раз повторяю, я решил вашу проблему.
examples.trans: I repeat once again, I solved your problem.

examples.text: Каждый день ты повторяешь одно и то же.
examples.trans: Every day you repeat the same thing.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to show', paired with 'показывать'.

examples.trans: Shall we show this to Anikeev?

examples.text: Ну, покажите руки. Что у вас за спиной?
examples.trans: Well, show me your hands. What is behind your back?

meanings.note: по порядку = in order; всё в порядке = everything is fine

examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order.

examples.text: Теперь давай всё по порядку. Скажи мне, сколько ты им должна?
examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order. Tell me, how much do you owe them?

meanings.en: to have a look, to take a look
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'смотреть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a look', forming an aspectual pair with 'смотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch (a film) through') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Я прекрасно понимаю = I understand perfectly
Secondary conversational sense ('wonderful!') (as a reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нет, лучше так: все говорят, а я делаю! Прекрасно.
examples.trans: No, better like this: everyone talks, while I do! Excellent.

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: refers back to the subject: 'он держит своё слово' = he keeps his word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: comparative of скоро used as adverb or particle

examples.trans: Let's go quickly to the studio!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лишком').

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'покойно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Его не будет часа два. Вы спокойно всё сделаете.
examples.trans: He'll be gone for about two hours. You'll do everything calmly.

справиться.gloss: to manage, to cope, to handle

meanings.note: often + с + instrumental, or used absolutely

examples.text: Мы за два года тут не справимся.
examples.trans: We won't manage here in two years.

examples.text: Конечно, не справитесь. Вы же не я.
examples.trans: Of course you won't manage. You're not me, after all.

examples.text: Мы обязательно справимся и с этим.
examples.trans: We will definitely cope with this too.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трогий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strict, stern').

examples.trans: How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

examples.text: У нас в школе очень строгий директор.
examples.trans: We have a very strict principal at our school.

examples.text: Ой, спина не разгибается! Какая вы строгая, Клавдия Викторовна.
examples.trans: Ow, my back won't straighten! How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'confident' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('sure, certain') (short form уверен / уверена) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный.
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident.
He answered in a calm, confident voice.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный. Что конкретно?
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident. What specifically?

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.en: to hear, catch the sound of
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'слышать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to hear', paired with 'слышать'.

examples.trans: I am glad to hear that.
I just want to hear the truth.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.en: to value, to appreciate, to esteem
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to value', forming an aspectual pair with 'оценить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Город высоко ценит вас и вашего мужа.
examples.trans: The city values you and your husband highly.

examples.text: Слушай, Лёля, я очень ценю, что ты приехала.
examples.trans: Listen, Lyolya, I really appreciate that you came.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
